infra.summary: There is no infrastructure-as-code in this repository. infra/modules/{core,groups,media,scale} exist as empty directories, and the modules are referenced only in comments. What deployment actually requires is legible from config/runtime.exs instead: four DynamoDB tables plus a by-user GSI, all supplied by name through environment variables that raise at boot when missing, an AWS region defaulting to ap-south-1, and an allow-list of browser origins. No instance classes, capacity modes, autoscaling bounds or memory limits exist anywhere in this repo, so nothing here can tell you what it costs or how far it scales.

resources.name: DynamoDB — messages
resources.detail: Partition conversation_id, sort id. Name from DYNAMO_MESSAGES_TABLE; capacity mode not declared in this repo.

resources.name: DynamoDB — conversations
resources.detail: Group and DM rows. Name from DYNAMO_CONVERSATIONS_TABLE.

resources.name: DynamoDB — memberships (+ by_user GSI)
resources.detail: Partition conversation_id; global secondary index on user_id drives the inbox. Names from DYNAMO_MEMBERSHIPS_TABLE and DYNAMO_MEMBERSHIPS_BY_USER_INDEX.

resources.name: DynamoDB — users directory
resources.detail: Partition username. Registration uniqueness is a conditional put. Name from DYNAMO_USERS_TABLE.

resources.name: media-service (external Go service)
resources.detail: Reached over HTTP with a bearer token from MEDIA_SERVICE_TOKEN; owns object storage and hands back presigned URLs. Lives outside this repository.

services.name: Inbox Channel
services.verdict: Joining your own inbox replays the full message history of every conversation you belong to, in order to compute a preview string and an unread count.
services.tierNote: The heaviest read path in the system, and the one every client hits on every connect — worth the full treatment.

services.name: Conversation Channel
services.verdict: Every message with an attachment blocks on a synchronous HTTP call to an external service before the durable write, and each message then fans out one inbox broadcast per member.
services.tierNote: The write path of the whole product, with an external dependency and per-member fan-out in it.

services.name: Media
services.verdict: GET /api/media/:id returns any media record to any caller with any x-user-id header — the code names this gap in a comment rather than enforcing it.
services.tierNote: A known authorisation hole plus the only external service call in the system.

services.name: Conversations
services.verdict: Membership changes do check that the caller is already a member before allowing them, which is more than the rest of the system does.
services.tierNote: Real authorisation logic and broadcast fan-out, but no external calls and no unbounded reads.

services.name: Directory Channel
services.verdict: Twenty-eight lines that trigger a full DynamoDB table scan every time any client connects, because the contact list is read with Scan rather than a query.
services.tierNote: Trivial code, non-trivial cost — the finding is in the module it calls, not in the channel itself.

services.name: Registration
services.verdict: Username uniqueness is a conditional put rather than a check-then-write, so two clients racing for the same name cannot both win.
services.tierNote: Small, but it is the only place in the system that resolves a race correctly, and worth recording as such.

services.name: Health
services.verdict: Returns a static ok without checking any dependency, which is the correct shape for a load balancer liveness probe.
services.tierNote: Ten lines with no branches. A deeper pass would be padding.

platformFindings.title: Identity is whatever the caller puts in x-user-id
platformFindings.breaks: Every authenticated REST route derives the caller's identity from a request header that is never verified against anything. Sending x-user-id: alice is sufficient to act as alice — create groups on her behalf, remove members from her conversations, and complete uploads as her. The socket has the same shape: the connect params supply user_id directly.
platformFindings.fix: Issue a signed token at registration and derive user_id from it in the plug and in UserSocket.connect/3, rather than from a client-supplied string. Until then, treat every 'only a member can…' check in the system as decorative, because the actor they compare against is attacker-chosen.

platformFindings.title: The websocket accepts any user_id offered at connect
platformFindings.breaks: UserSocket.connect/3 assigns whatever user_id the client sends. Channel authorisation downstream — inbox 'can only join your own inbox', DM membership, message sender attribution — all compare against this value, so an attacker who names themselves as someone else passes all of it and can read that person's conversations.
platformFindings.fix: Verify a signed token in connect/3 (Phoenix.Token.verify against the endpoint's secret_key_base) and assign the user_id it carries. check_origin restricts which pages may open a socket, but not who the connecting client claims to be.

platformFindings.title: Every read path uses the raising ExAws call, so a DynamoDB blip crashes the channel
platformFindings.breaks: The list and query paths call ExAws.request! rather than request. A throttled or failed DynamoDB call raises inside the channel process, which takes down the join or the message handler rather than returning an error the client can retry. Under exactly the throttling that a Scan-per-connect makes likely, clients see dropped sockets instead of a degraded contact list.
platformFindings.fix: Use ExAws.request/1 in the read paths and map {:error, _} to an empty or partial result, so a Dynamo hiccup degrades the list instead of killing the connection.

platformFindings.title: Deployment shape exists only as environment variables and empty directories
platformFindings.breaks: config/runtime.exs raises at boot for four table names and reads a region, and comments point at infra/modules/core, /groups and /media as the things that provision them — but those directories are empty. Nothing in this repository records capacity mode, autoscaling bounds, replica count or memory limits, so cost and scaling cannot be answered from the code, and a fresh deploy has no reproducible starting point.
platformFindings.fix: Commit the Terraform for the four tables and the by_user GSI, or state plainly in the README that infrastructure lives elsewhere and link to it.

platformFindings.title: The tests exercise the in-memory adapters; the DynamoDB ones ship unexercised
platformFindings.breaks: All 43 tests pass, but the store, directory and conversations suites test the Memory implementations, which are the dev and test defaults. The Dynamo implementations — the ones that actually run in production, including the conditional-put uniqueness guard and the GSI query — have no test of their own. A regression in the key condition or the condition expression would pass CI.
platformFindings.fix: Add a suite for the Dynamo adapters against DynamoDB Local, so the paths that run in production are the paths that are tested.

topology.summary: Sending a message is one durable write surrounded by four optional round trips: an external HTTP call to verify an attachment before the write, and two DynamoDB queries plus a per-member broadcast loop after the sender has already been acked. Membership is the only authorisation, and the identity it checks comes from a client-supplied string.
topology.loadNote: Load is not measured. There is no load test, no benchmark and no telemetry export in this repository — Plug.Telemetry emits events but nothing subscribes to them. Every scaling statement here is derived from the code's call structure, not from observation.

nodes.label: ConversationChannel
nodes.sublabel: one process per member per tab

steps.title: ① The socket carries an unverified identity
steps.desc: The sender's user_id is whatever the client passed in the socket's connect params. Everything below — 'does this attachment belong to you', 'are you a member of this conversation' — compares against that string.

steps.title: ② Attachment check blocks the write
steps.desc: A message carrying media_id triggers a synchronous HTTP call to media-service before anything durable happens. No timeout is set, so the default governs, and a slow media-service turns into a stalled message send.

steps.title: ③ One put, then the message exists
steps.desc: The message is written before any attempt to push it, so delivery survives a dead socket. The id is a millisecond timestamp plus a per-node counter, which sorts correctly within one conversation without a global clock.

steps.title: ④⑤ Ack the sender, then one broadcast for everyone
steps.desc: The sending tab gets its optimistic id swapped for the real one. Delivery to every other member and every other tab is a single PubSub broadcast on the conversation topic, not one write per recipient.

steps.title: ⑥⑦ Then it does the expensive part
steps.desc: After the ack, the channel re-queries the conversation and its members, then emits one inbox broadcast per member so their rooms list updates without joining the conversation. Two round trips plus N broadcasts, on every message.

security.title: The sender of a message is whoever the socket said it was
security.breaks: user_id is taken straight from the connect params and assigned to the socket. Every message written by this channel is attributed to that string, and DM authorisation is a substring match against it, so a client that connects as someone else can both read that person's DMs and post as them.
security.fix: Sign a token at registration and verify it in connect/3 with Phoenix.Token.verify, then assign the user_id it carries. check_origin limits which page may open the socket, not who the socket claims to be.

security.title: Nothing limits how fast one socket can send messages
security.breaks: handle_in has no throttle, and neither does the socket. Each accepted message costs one Dynamo put, two Dynamo queries and N broadcasts, so a single client in a loop multiplies straight into write capacity and cluster-wide PubSub traffic for every member.
security.fix: Add a per-socket token bucket in handle_in and reject over-budget sends with the existing rejected ack path, which the client already handles.

reliability.title: A slow media-service stalls every message that carries an attachment
reliability.breaks: Req.request is called with no receive timeout and no retry or circuit-breaker policy. Because validate_media runs before the durable write, a media-service that is slow rather than down holds the channel process open per in-flight send, and the sender sees neither an ack nor a rejection.
reliability.fix: Set an explicit receive_timeout on the Req call and treat a timeout as a rejected ack. Better still, write the message first and verify the attachment asynchronously, so the durable path never depends on a third service being up.

reliability.title: The inbox fan-out runs after the ack, so its failures are invisible
reliability.breaks: The two queries and the per-member broadcasts happen after the sender has been told the message was sent. If the conversations query raises — and it uses the raising ExAws call — the channel process dies with the message already durably written and the sender already acked. Members' inbox rows silently do not update.
reliability.fix: Move the fan-out behind a supervised task with its own error handling, and use the non-raising ExAws.request so a Dynamo blip degrades the inbox preview instead of killing the channel.

sequence.title: Full sequence — one message sent into a conversation
sequence.blurb: A message carrying an attachment waits on an HTTP round trip to an external Go service before anything durable is written. After the sender is acked, the channel keeps working: it re-reads the conversation and its members, then emits one inbox broadcast per member.

intro.sub: client_msg_id, body, optional media_id — over the already-open socket

summary.title: round trips for one message with an attachment:
lines: 1 HTTP call to media-service, blocking, before any write
1 DynamoDB put, then 2 DynamoDB queries after the ack
1 conversation broadcast + N inbox broadcasts, where N is the member count
load is not measured — no load test exists in this repository

items.title: Stop re-querying the conversation and its members after every message
items.costsToday: Two extra DynamoDB queries per message sent — one Query on the conversations table and one on the memberships table — purely to build the inbox preview. In a busy group these are the same two rows read over and over, and they run after the sender has already been acked, so they buy no latency for the sender and only consume read capacity.
items.gain: Removes 2 of the 4 DynamoDB round trips on the send path, leaving the put and nothing else. Read capacity on the conversations and memberships tables stops scaling with message volume and scales with membership change instead.
items.how: Cache the member list in the channel's socket assigns at join time — the channel already loads it there — and invalidate it on the member_added and member_removed broadcasts the channel is already subscribed to.
items.risk: A member added while a tab is open would be missed until that broadcast lands, so the invalidation has to be wired before the cache is trusted.

items.title: Put an explicit timeout on the media-service call
items.costsToday: Req is called with no receive timeout, and the call sits before the durable write. A media-service that is slow rather than down holds one channel process per in-flight send with the sender receiving neither an ack nor a rejection, and there is no metric that would show it happening.
items.gain: Turns an unbounded stall into a bounded failure the client already knows how to render — the rejected ack path exists and is tested.
items.how: Pass receive_timeout to Req.request in Wavelink.Media.request/3 and map a timeout onto the existing {:error, reason} clause, which already produces 'could not verify attachment'.
items.referenceNote: Every integration point needs a timeout; without one, a slow remote service is worse than a dead one because callers pile up behind it.

items.title: Write the message first, verify the attachment after
items.costsToday: Message durability currently depends on a second service being reachable. Any message with an attachment is lost entirely — never written, only rejected — when media-service is down, even though the message body itself has nothing to do with media-service.
items.gain: Sends stop failing for a reason unrelated to the message. The blocking HTTP call leaves the write path, which removes the only external dependency from the one operation that must not fail.
items.how: Write the message with the media_id and a pending marker, ack the sender, then verify ownership in a supervised task and emit a correction broadcast if the attachment turns out not to belong to the sender.
items.risk: A window opens where a message references an attachment the sender does not own. That is acceptable only because media-service still refuses to hand out bytes to a non-member — confirm that before shipping this.

items.title: Use the non-raising ExAws call on the read paths
items.costsToday: Every list and query path calls ExAws.request!, so one throttled DynamoDB read raises inside the channel process and drops the socket. The user's symptom is a disconnected chat, not a missing preview, and the cause is invisible from the client.
items.gain: A throttled read degrades one inbox preview instead of dropping a live connection, which also removes the reconnect storm that follows a throttling episode.
items.how: Swap ExAws.request! for ExAws.request in the read functions and return an empty list on {:error, _}, leaving the write paths raising as they are.
items.referenceNote: Failures should degrade the feature that failed, not propagate into unrelated parts of the system.

optimise.note: Ordered by gain per unit of effort. The first two are afternoons and remove work from the hot path; the third is the one that stops the send path depending on a third service being up.

topology.summary: Three thin endpoints in front of an external Go service. Two of them derive the owner from the authenticated header and pass it down for enforcement; the third returns any media record, and a signed URL for its bytes, to anyone who sends any x-user-id. The gap is documented in a comment above the function rather than closed.
topology.loadNote: Load is not measured. No load test, benchmark or telemetry backend exists in this repository. What can be said from the code is structural: file bytes never pass through this process, so upload size does not translate into memory pressure here.

steps.title: ①② Owner comes from the plug, not the body
steps.desc: owner_id is read from conn.assigns, which the RequireUserId plug set, so a client cannot claim to be uploading on someone else's behalf by editing the JSON. That is the right shape — its weakness is one layer up, in what the plug trusts.

steps.title: ③ Bytes go straight to storage
steps.desc: The browser PUTs the file to a presigned URL. This backend never proxies file content, so a large upload costs it nothing in memory or connection time — the only thing it handles is small JSON.

steps.title: ④⑤ Completion is enforced downstream
steps.desc: The completion call carries owner_id and media-service returns 403 when it does not match the upload it was created for, so a client cannot finalise someone else's slot.

steps.title: ⑥⑦ Read-back checks nothing
steps.desc: show/2 passes the id straight through with no owner and no membership check, and media-service is not the layer that knows about conversation membership. Any authenticated caller — which here means any caller at all — can resolve any media id to a signed URL.

security.title: GET /api/media/:id hands any attachment to any caller
security.breaks: show/2 performs no ownership or membership check — it forwards the id to media-service and returns the record along with a short-lived signed URL for the bytes. Media ids are sortable, sequential-looking strings generated from a timestamp, so they can be walked rather than guessed. The practical result is that every attachment ever uploaded to any private conversation is readable by anyone who can reach the API.
security.fix: Build the media_id → conversation_id index the comment says is missing — the association already exists on the message row — and have show/2 confirm the caller is a member of that conversation before resolving. Until then, treat every uploaded file as public.

security.title: The owner of an upload is an unverified header
security.breaks: create/2 and complete/2 correctly refuse to take owner_id from the request body, taking it from conn.assigns instead — but the plug that fills conn.assigns copies it verbatim out of the x-user-id header with no verification. The careful part of the design is defeated by the layer beneath it: uploads can be created and completed as any user by changing one header.
security.fix: Derive user_id from a signed token in the plug. Every 'the owner comes from the plug, not the body' guarantee in this controller depends on that one change.

security.title: size_bytes is forwarded without a ceiling on this side
security.breaks: create/2 checks that content_type and size_bytes are present but not that size_bytes is a number, or within any bound, before asking media-service for a slot. Whatever limit exists lives entirely in the external service, so this API cannot state its own upload policy and a change there silently changes behaviour here.
security.fix: Validate size_bytes as a positive integer under an explicit maximum in the controller, so the limit is visible in the code that advertises the endpoint.

reliability.title: Every call to media-service is untimed
reliability.breaks: Req.request is invoked with a method, a URL, an auth header and sometimes a body — no receive timeout, no retry policy, no circuit breaker. All three routes here inherit that, and so does the attachment check on the message send path, so one slow external service degrades two services at once.
reliability.fix: Set an explicit receive_timeout in Wavelink.Media.request/3. It is a single change and it bounds every caller, because every caller goes through this one function.

reliability.title: Every transport failure becomes an indistinguishable 502
reliability.breaks: The catch-all clause maps every {:error, reason} — DNS failure, connection refused, timeout, malformed response — onto the same 502 with the same body. Nothing is logged at the point of failure, so an outage and a misconfigured URL look identical from both the client and the server side.
reliability.fix: Log the reason before responding and keep the flat 502 for the client. One log line turns an opaque error class into a diagnosable one.

sequence.title: Full sequence — one attachment, from slot to read-back
sequence.blurb: File bytes never touch this backend: it brokers a presigned URL and the browser uploads straight to storage. The read-back at the end is the problem — it returns any media record, plus a signed URL for the bytes, to any caller who supplies any x-user-id.

summary.title: round trips for one attachment:
lines: 3 calls to media-service — create, complete, read — plus one direct browser-to-storage PUT
0 bytes of file content pass through this backend, by design
1 of the 3 endpoints performs no authorisation beyond 'a header was present'
load is not measured — no load test exists in this repository

items.title: Make GET /api/media/:id check conversation membership
items.costsToday: Every attachment in every private conversation is readable by any caller. Ids are derived from a timestamp and sort lexicographically, so they enumerate rather than resist guessing, and the endpoint returns a signed URL for the bytes, not just metadata. There is no log line that would show it happening.
items.gain: Closes the only route in this service that performs no authorisation at all, and makes the two routes that already do their part meaningful.
items.how: Add a media_id → conversation_id index at the point the message is written — Store.put_message already receives both — then have show/2 look it up and call Conversations.member?/2 before resolving. The comment above show/2 names this same missing index.
items.risk: Attachments written before the index exists have no entry, so decide deliberately whether those fail closed or stay readable during a backfill.
items.referenceNote: Broken access control — an object reference accepted from the client without checking the caller is entitled to that object.

items.title: Put an explicit timeout on the media-service call
items.costsToday: All three routes here and the attachment check on the message send path funnel through one untimed Req call. A slow media-service therefore stalls uploads and message sends simultaneously, with no metric that would surface it.
items.gain: One change bounds every caller in the system, because every caller goes through this single function.
items.how: Pass receive_timeout to Req.request in Wavelink.Media.request/3 and let the existing {:error, reason} clause carry the result.
items.referenceNote: Every integration point needs a timeout; without one, a slow remote service is worse than a dead one because callers pile up behind it.

items.title: Log the reason before collapsing it into a 502
items.costsToday: A refused connection, a DNS failure, a timeout and a malformed response all produce the identical 502 body and leave no trace. During an incident there is nothing to distinguish 'media-service is down' from 'the URL is wrong', which is the difference between a rollback and a config fix.
items.gain: Turns one opaque error class into a diagnosable one for the cost of a single line.
items.how: Log the reason in the catch-all respond/3 clause before rendering the 502, keeping the client-facing body exactly as it is.
items.referenceNote: Failures should be diagnosable from telemetry alone, without reproducing them.

items.title: Validate size_bytes before brokering a slot
items.costsToday: The controller checks that size_bytes is present, not that it is a positive integer or within any limit, so this API's upload policy is whatever the external service happens to enforce today. A change there silently changes what this endpoint accepts, and neither side's limit is visible in this repository.
items.gain: Makes the endpoint's own contract explicit and rejects oversized requests before they cost a round trip to media-service.
items.how: Match size_bytes as a positive integer under a named module attribute in create/2 and return 422 otherwise, alongside the existing content_type check.

optimise.note: The first item is not really an optimisation — it is the one thing on this list that should be done before this service is exposed to anyone. The rest are ordinary.
